kp.k: Superstar markets combine concentrated output and exceptional rewards
kp.d: Rosen develops a theoretical account of markets in which relatively few talented sellers command large audiences and disproportionately high earnings. His examples include entertainment, textbooks, research and professional services. The opening illustrations rely on informed opinion and observations rather than systematic data, whose collection he describes as difficult. This is a historical economic framework, not a study of AI.

kp.k: Imperfect substitution magnifies the rewards of superior talent
kp.d: Rosen argues that greater quantities of inferior service may not compensate consumers for lower quality. This supports convex returns to talent, stretching the upper tail of earnings relative to the talent distribution. His illustrations include outstanding singers, a surgeon who is 10 percent more successful in saving lives, and the value of legal talent in high-stakes litigation. These are explanatory examples, not measured estimates of professional returns.

kp.k: Joint consumption explains concentration beyond earnings inequality
kp.d: Imperfect substitution alone does not explain why output concentrates among a few sellers. Rosen adds technology permitting a performance or written work to reach many customers without proportionate increases in production costs. Joint consumption combined with differentiated talent allows superior sellers to serve very large markets. Unlike a pure public good, the seller retains property rights and can exclude nonpaying consumers.

kp.k: The model abstracts from uncertainty and preference complexity
kp.d: The formal model represents talent and charisma through a single quality index, assumes a fixed and costlessly observable talent distribution, and models assignment between utility-maximizing buyers and profit-maximizing sellers. Its quantity-quality formulation deliberately simplifies preferences for variety, multidimensional exposure and market boundaries. Reputation is discussed as a possible extension, but its formation is not modeled.

kp.k: Consumption costs influence buyers' quality choices
kp.d: Consumers face both the purchase price and a fixed cost per unit of consumption, potentially reflecting time valued at the wage rate. Higher consumption costs favor purchasing greater quality rather than more quantity. With heterogeneous consumption costs, Rosen sketches sorting between buyers and sellers and a convex price-quality relationship that strengthens superstar outcomes; he explicitly stops short of a full analysis of that extension.

kp.k: Congestion and limited time constrain professional market scale
kp.d: Rosen distinguishes internal production costs from external diseconomies that reduce service quality as a seller's market expands. Reproduction or larger venues can dilute a performance; in professional services, a larger patient load can reduce direct contact and increase waiting. The model therefore encompasses one-to-one services as well as reproducible output. An important assumption is that superior talent deteriorates less rapidly with market size.

kp.k: Price and volume jointly amplify income differences
kp.d: With only internal diseconomies, more talented sellers charge higher prices and supply more, creating convex earnings even under a linear efficiency-units specification. In Rosen's quadratic-cost example, twice the talent produces four times the earnings. With external diseconomies, his illustrative specifications yield four times the market and eight times the earnings, or sixteen times the earnings, for twice the talent. These are conditional mathematical examples, not empirical estimates.

kp.k: Concentration does not necessarily imply monopoly rents
kp.d: In the limiting case of pure joint consumption without diseconomies, one highest-quality seller serves the entire market. Potential entry can nevertheless constrain pricing: when competing talent is arbitrarily close, equilibrium rents disappear. A superstar separated from the nearest competitor by a finite quality gap can earn a small premium per transaction but large total rents through market scale. Rosen also identifies inefficiency in this limiting example and notes conditions bounding it elsewhere in the analysis.

kp.k: Demand expansion disproportionately benefits the most talented
kp.d: In the common-consumption-cost model, more consumers or stronger demand raise the equilibrium service price, expand existing sellers' output and attract less talented entrants. Existing sellers earn higher rents, with the largest gains accruing to the most talented, increasing earnings skew. Rosen consequently predicts that operating in larger markets is especially lucrative for superior talent, including doctors, lawyers and professional athletes.

kp.k: Technology's distributional effects depend on demand elasticity
kp.d: Reductions in internal costs or congestion expand service supply, lower its equilibrium price and benefit consumers, but seller outcomes depend on demand elasticity. Sufficiently elastic demand permits rents and their concentration at the top to increase. Lower internal diseconomies induce entry, whereas a sufficiently large reduction in external diseconomies can eliminate less talented sellers. With inelastic demand, seller numbers decline and effects on rents are ambiguous. Rosen connects these mechanisms to historical communications technologies and expanded markets for professional and information services, rather than to AI.

kp.k: Rising time costs can further concentrate rewards
kp.d: An increase in the fixed consumption cost reduces sellers' unit prices at a given full service price and shifts supply inward. In equilibrium, the full service price rises, less talented sellers leave, and the rent distribution favors greater talent. Rosen further argues that consumption time costs correlate with consumer earnings, so simultaneous demand growth can reinforce earnings skew, while creating incentives for time-saving innovations such as consumption at home.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Rosen explains how differences in talent, combined with technologies that expand sellers' reach, can concentrate output and earnings among superstars. This is a cross-domain economic argument, not a claim about AI.
pts.d: Rosen's 1981 article argues that imperfect substitution between sellers of different quality produces disproportionately large earnings differences relative to talent differences. Concentration of output additionally depends on production technology: joint consumption lets a seller serve many buyers without proportionately increasing production costs. Together, these mechanisms can give highly talented sellers both large markets and large incomes. Larger overall demand raises earnings for incumbent sellers, with the greatest gains going to the most talented, while also permitting less talented entrants. Reductions in costs or congestion lower the equilibrium price of services and benefit consumers, but their effects on seller earnings and entry depend on demand elasticity and the type of diseconomy reduced. With sufficiently elastic demand, technological improvements can increase seller rents and concentration of earnings at the top. Reduced internal diseconomies encourage entry; sufficiently reduced external diseconomies can instead displace less talented sellers. Rosen also argues that higher consumer time and effort costs favor purchasing higher quality rather than greater quantity. He applies the framework to entertainment, publishing, sports and professional services, with occasional legal examples, but does not discuss AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal basis is a formal equilibrium model, supplemented by illustrative observations and historical examples rather than systematic empirical testing.
pts.d: Rosen develops an assignment model linking buyers to sellers, specifying preferences over quantity and quality, sellers' production and congestion costs, and equilibrium price, market size and revenue schedules. Convex revenue functions and comparative-static results provide the analytical basis for the claims. Numerical illustrations show how particular functional assumptions can magnify talent differences into larger market-size and earnings differences; these are model examples, not measured effects. Opening illustrations include an informed-opinion estimate of roughly two hundred full-time US comedians, the small number and unequal earnings of classical soloists, and concentration in textbook sales and research citations. Historical discussion identifies broadcasting, recordings and communications improvements as examples of expanded reach. Rosen acknowledges difficulty obtaining systematic data. The conclusion quotes Alfred Marshall as historical context; Marshall's statements are not independent empirical findings by Rosen. No AI experiments, legal-technology benchmarks or measured effects on legal employment are offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: These are equilibrium and comparative-static claims, with historical technological illustrations through 1981, not dated forecasts of AI adoption or displacement.
pts.d: The model assumes a fixed distribution of talent that agents can observe without cost. Its main closed-form treatment assumes a common fixed consumption cost across buyers; the discussion of heterogeneous consumers argues that sorting can strengthen the qualitative conclusions but does not supply a full analysis. Large output concentration requires sufficiently strong scale economies; professional services remain constrained by seller time and congestion. The prediction that reduced diseconomies increase seller rents is conditional on sufficiently elastic demand. With inelastic demand, seller numbers fall and effects on rents are ambiguous. In the extreme case of pure joint consumption, a single seller can serve the entire market, but concentration alone does not guarantee rents: very close potential competitors can eliminate them, whereas a distinctly superior outlier can earn substantial rents over a large market. The article closes with an open question about future communications technologies rather than a quantified forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The model concerns individual service sellers and their customers, especially top talent whose reach can expand; it does not analyze AI vendors, law-firm staffing or legal occupations as employment categories.
pts.d: Top performers, authors, researchers, athletes and professional practitioners can obtain disproportionately greater earnings as their markets expand. Less talented sellers may gain entry when demand grows or internal production constraints ease, but may lose business or exit when congestion barriers fall sufficiently or demand is inelastic. Consumers benefit from lower service prices after reductions in diseconomies, and those facing greater time costs select higher-quality sellers. In professional services, expansion can mean less direct contact and longer waits, which customers may accept in exchange for greater practitioner quality. Rosen includes lawyers among professionals expected to locate more frequently in larger cities and uses high-stakes litigation to illustrate willingness to pay for legal talent. These are claims about practitioner quality and market scale, not findings about legal AI, law-firm business models, or access to justice.
